Social Studies.contentMarkdown:
**Course link and limits:** NYC Passport Grade 6 Unit 3 is titled **Comparative World Religions**. Its public overview says students study the development, spread, and continued practice of belief systems; examine primary and secondary sources, artifacts, and images; compare Confucianism with Taoism; study representative Buddhist and Hindu art; and compare shared characteristics of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. It describes an informational comparison essay as the unit assessment. The full teacher materials require NYC DOE access. This guide uses the public unit description and other public sources; it does not claim to reproduce Passport lessons or confirm Ditmas J.H.S. 62's current pacing. [NYC Passport Unit 3 overview](https://www.weteachnyc.org/resources/resource/passport-social-studies-grade-6-unit-3/).

**State scope:** NYSED Standard **6.4, Comparative World Religions (ca. 2000 B.C.E.–ca. 630 C.E.)**, asks students to compare where and when Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Buddhism, Hinduism, and Confucianism developed; founders, if any; major ideas and practices; and sacred writings or important texts. It also asks how belief systems can shape social order and gender roles. The dates are the framework's study window. They do **not** mean that any tradition ended then. [New York State K–8 Social Studies Framework, Grade 6, Standard 6.4](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/standards-instruction/ss-framework-k-8a2.pdf); [NYSED standard detail](https://nylearns.org/module/standards/Tools/StandardDetail?LinkStandardId=0&StandardId=189312).

#### Read this first: compare carefully, without flattening people

People inside one tradition can hold different beliefs, follow different practices, read texts in different ways, and live in different cultures. Traditions also change over time. A fair history question names a place, time, group, and source: **Which people? Where? When? What source supports the claim?** Harvard Divinity School's Religion and Public Life project teaches those habits and distinguishes academic study from devotional teaching. This guide studies what sources say; it does not ask students to accept or reject anyone's beliefs. [Harvard Religion and Public Life, “Religion in Context”](https://rpl.hds.harvard.edu/religion-context); [Harvard RPL, “Core Principles”](https://rpl.hds.harvard.edu/what-we-do/our-approach/core-principles).

“Founder” also needs care. Some traditions are connected to a named historical teacher; others developed over long periods and do not have one founder. NYSED's wording “if any” makes room for that difference. Confucianism is included in the state comparison, but it is often described as an ethical and philosophical tradition as well as a religious tradition. Do not force all six into the same definition.

#### Six concise comparison notes

Use these as starting points, not complete definitions. The Harvard introductory profiles are adapted from *On Common Ground: World Religions in America* and repeatedly warn readers to account for internal diversity and historical change. The dates below are broad teaching estimates, not exact founding days.

#### Key words in simple English

- **B.C.E. / C.E.**: year labels used here for dates before and after year 1. They refer to the same year numbers often written B.C. / A.D.
- **Source**: something used to learn about a subject, such as an object, map, text, photograph, or researched article.
- **Context**: who, where, and when; these details help explain what a source can tell us.
- **Internal diversity**: differences among people and groups within one tradition.
- **Levant**: a region on the eastern side of the Mediterranean Sea; its borders change depending on the time and source.
- **Sangha**: a Buddhist monastic community of monks and nuns.
- **Bhikkhu / bhikkhuni**: a Buddhist monk / nun in the Theravada tradition discussed in the Sri Lanka case.
- **Theravada / Mahayana**: names for two large Buddhist traditions; each includes different communities and histories.
- **Ordination**: a formal ceremony that gives someone a recognized role in a religious community.
- **Dasa sil mātāvo**: the local name used in the Harvard case study for a community of Sri Lankan Buddhist women practitioners.
- **Finial**: an ornament placed at the top of an object; these finials were placed on the staves of a Torah scroll.
- **Social order**: the roles, rules, and relationships that shape how a society is organized.
- **Inference**: a conclusion a reader draws from clues; it should be labeled and supported, not confused with a source's exact words.
- **Pilgrimage**: a religious journey to a place that is important to a community.

| Tradition | Place and time used in this comparison | Founder, if any | Text examples and practices to investigate |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hindu traditions** | South Asia; developed over a long period, so there is no single founding date for all Hindu traditions. | No single founder. | The Vedas, Upanishads, and *Bhagavad Gita* are among many important texts. Practices and beliefs vary; investigate one named community, text, or practice at a time. |
| **Judaism** | Ancient communities of the Levant; its history continued through many places and periods. | No single historical founder in the same sense as a movement centered on one teacher. | The Torah is central within the larger Tanakh; later Jewish interpretation and practice also draw on rabbinic texts. Sabbath, study, prayer, and festivals are examples, not a checklist followed identically by all Jews. |
| **Buddhism** | South Asia, around the first millennium B.C.E.; the exact dates of the Buddha's life are debated by scholars. | Siddhartha Gautama, remembered as the Buddha, is the central teacher associated with its beginnings. | Buddhist collections differ among communities. The Met object caption connects the Four Noble Truths with the Buddha's teaching; practices such as ethical training and meditation vary across Buddhist traditions. |
| **Confucian traditions** | China; Kongzi (Confucius) lived traditionally from 551 to 479 B.C.E. | Kongzi is a key teacher, but later people built and reshaped Confucian thought. | The *Analects* records sayings and conversations associated with Confucius and his followers. Study learning, ritual, humane conduct, relationships, and public service in historical context. Whether to classify Confucianism as a religion, philosophy, or both depends on the question and context. |
| **Christianity** | Began in the first century C.E. in Roman Judea and spread through many regions. | Jesus is the central figure; the tradition formed through the lives and teachings of Jesus' followers. | The Christian Bible contains the Old and New Testaments. Christian communities interpret scripture and practice worship in varied ways; Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions are broad groupings, not the whole story. |
| **Islam** | Began in seventh-century Arabia and spread into many societies. | Muslims understand Muhammad as God's prophet; Islam's early community formed around his preaching. | The Qur'an is Islam's central sacred text. Prayer, giving, fasting, and pilgrimage are important practices for many Muslims, with differences in interpretation and practice among communities. |

**Important limits on the table:** “South Asia,” “ancient Levant,” “first century,” and “seventh century” are broad location and time clues, not borders around a living tradition. A list of a few texts cannot stand for every scripture or interpretation. Do not say “all Hindus,” “all Jews,” “all Buddhists,” “all Confucians,” “all Christians,” or “all Muslims” unless a reliable source supports that precise claim. For more detail, use the Harvard introductory profiles for five traditions and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Confucius; check each specific claim against its source. [Harvard RPL introductory profiles](https://rpl.hds.harvard.edu/HarvardXResourceLibrary); [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Confucius”](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/confucius/).

#### A sourced case: Buddhist women's ordination in Sri Lanka

Harvard Religion and Public Life's case study follows a specific debate in Sri Lanka; it is not a statement about every Buddhist community. The study reports that a community of ordained Buddhist nuns on the island ended around the 11th century. Women who were not formally members of the monastic sangha still served as respected religious practitioners. In the early 20th century, a community of women known as *dasa sil mātāvo* became an important part of Sri Lankan Buddhist life.

In 1988 and 1996, Sri Lankan women received ordination as bhikkhunis with help from Mahayana nuns from East Asia. The case study describes mixed reactions. Some Sri Lankan monks questioned whether the ceremonies met Theravada rules; some women also questioned whether ordination would give them more authority or bind them to rules they considered unequal. Other women chose ordination because they thought recognition as members of the sangha could improve their status. The source reports that hundreds of Sri Lankan Buddhist women have since been formally ordained, while reactions in other Theravada communities have remained different.

This case can support a narrow claim: in a particular place and time, different people interpreted rules and institutions differently, and those decisions affected women's religious roles and access to recognition. It cannot prove that “Buddhism treats women one way” everywhere. Separate what the case study reports from your own judgment about fairness. [Harvard RPL, “The Ordination of Nuns in Sri Lanka”](https://rpl.hds.harvard.edu/religion-context/case-studies/gender/ordination-nuns-sri-lanka).

#### Visual source gallery: museum objects are evidence, not symbols for everyone

These six photographs are public-domain collection images from The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Each object comes from a particular place and time. A museum object can show materials, writing, design, and one use described by its curator. By itself, it cannot show what every member of a tradition believed or practiced. Open each object page, read its caption, and keep the caption's limits beside your observation. The Met's Open Access API marks the six images below as public domain.

**Judaism — Torah finials, Galicia, 1775–90.** The museum says these ornaments were placed on the staves holding a Torah scroll. The object records one synagogue practice and a particular community's metalwork; it does not represent all Jewish art or worship. [Met object record](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/903518).

![Pair of silver Torah finials from Galicia, dated 1775–90, in The Met collection.](https://images.metmuseum.org/CRDImages/es/web-large/DP-34439-001.jpg)

**Christianity — Syrian processional cross, sixth century.** The Met describes this silver cross as an object carried in church processions and displayed in churches. The catalog places it in a specific Syrian setting. [Met object record](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/468349).

![A sixth-century Syrian silver processional cross in The Met collection.](https://images.metmuseum.org/CRDImages/md/web-large/DP-14824-003.jpg)

**Hindu traditions — Shiva as Lord of Dance, Tamil Nadu, late 12th–early 13th century.** The curator explains several features and their meanings within this specific image, including the drum and fire held by Shiva and a halo around the figure. The museum says images of this type were carried in processions during festivals. This is one work from one region and period. [Met object record](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/39329).

![A bronze image of Shiva as Lord of Dance from Tamil Nadu in The Met collection.](https://images.metmuseum.org/CRDImages/as/web-large/DP221497.jpg)

**Buddhism — seated Buddha from Nalanda, Bihar, late 10th–11th century.** The Met identifies the figure's hand touching the earth as an image of the moment of enlightenment. Its caption names the Four Noble Truths and identifies two accompanying figures. The caption describes this sculpture; it does not prove that every Buddhist image looks this way. [Met object record](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/38122).

![A seated Buddha touching the earth in a sculpture from Nalanda, Bihar.](https://images.metmuseum.org/CRDImages/as/web-large/6%20DP310502r3_61A.jpg)

**Islam — a Qur'an section made in China, 17th–18th century.** The Met says the manuscript uses Sini script and notes that early surviving Chinese Qur'ans were connected with Chinese Sunni Muslim communities called Hui. Its decoration is evidence of one manuscript tradition in one place and period, not a rule for every Qur'an. [Met object record](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/890784).

![An illuminated page from a Qur'an manuscript made in China, shown in The Met collection.](https://images.metmuseum.org/CRDImages/is/web-large/LC-2022_496_Interior_2.jpg)

**Confucian traditions — *Life of Confucius*, illustrated books, China, probably late Qing dynasty.** The Met catalogs this as four volumes of woodblock-printed books. It is a later representation of Confucius, not an object from his lifetime and not the *Analects* itself. [Met object record](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/60773).

![An illustrated woodblock-printed book set titled Life of Confucius in The Met collection.](https://images.metmuseum.org/CRDImages/as/web-large/CIB20a-d_d1.jpg)

#### Locate the broad regions

Use this current world outline to mark approximate regions in the table. It is based on Natural Earth data and shows modern political borders; those borders are **not** the borders of ancient states. Mark broad regions and coastlines only. Do not draw a precise “birthplace” from this map. [Wikimedia Commons map record and license](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BlankMap-Equirectangular.svg).

![A blank equirectangular world map with modern country outlines, based on Natural Earth data.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/BlankMap-Equirectangular.svg/1920px-BlankMap-Equirectangular.svg.png)

#### Five study sessions — 50–60 minutes each

| Day | Focus and steps | Work to save |
|---|---|---|
| **1 — Place and time** | 8 min: read the scope note and mark “study window” versus “tradition ended.” 12 min: locate South Asia, the Levant, China, Roman Judea, and Arabia on a classroom Eastern Hemisphere map. 15 min: place broad date clues from the comparison table on a timeline. 15 min: read the six comparison notes and circle any claim that needs a source. 5 min: exit question. | A labeled map and timeline. Beside each location, write the name of the source that supports it. Use “approximate” where the source gives a broad or debated date. |
| **2 — Texts, teachers, and practices** | 10 min: reread the six table rows. 15 min: sort the examples into “named teacher,” “no single founder,” “text example,” and “practice example.” 15 min: read the Harvard profile preface about diversity and change. 15 min: choose two traditions and explain what extra source would be needed before making a broad claim. | A comparison chart with two rows. Put a source clue beside each fact and one “what this does not prove” note under each row. |
| **3 — Read museum images as sources** | 5 min: review the image-reading steps below. 25 min: study the six Met images and captions; choose three for close analysis. 15 min: record visible detail, catalog fact, and a question. 10 min: compare one pair without claiming the objects show the same belief or use. | Three evidence cards: image detail; exact catalog fact in your own words; one limit or question. Include the object title and date/place. |
| **4 — Beliefs and social life** | 10 min: read NYSED's 6.4 questions about shared values, social order, and gender roles. 15 min: read the Sri Lanka case above and mark its dates, groups, and different views. 15 min: build a timeline from the case study. 10 min: compare the reasons some women sought ordination with the reasons others did not. 5 min: revise one overgeneralized sentence into a careful claim. | A claim/evidence/limit chart. Never use one person's statement, one object, or one era as proof about every person in a tradition. |
| **5 — Write and check a comparison** | 8 min: choose two traditions and narrow the comparison to one question (origin, text, practice, art, or a sourced historical effect). 12 min: plan a claim and gather two source details. 20 min: write the comparison paragraph below. 10 min: check every sentence for time, place, and source. 5 min: peer review or self-check. | A revised, source-based paragraph with the comparison checklist completed. |

**Image-reading routine:** (1) Look silently for 30 seconds. (2) Write two details that can be seen, such as material, shape, writing, color, or position. (3) Read the museum title, date, place, and caption. (4) Add one fact the caption gives. (5) State one thing the image cannot establish. Keep “I see” separate from “the museum says” and “I infer.”

**Writing frame:** “In [named place/time], [tradition A] and [tradition B] can be compared through [specific question]. Source A says ____. Source B says ____. One similarity/difference is ____. These sources support this limited claim because ____. They do not show that every member of either tradition ____.” Use two distinct sources and name them in the paragraph.

**End-of-week check:** A strong response (a) answers one focused comparison question; (b) uses at least two correct, named source details; (c) identifies a similarity or difference; (d) gives time or place where relevant; (e) separates evidence from inference; and (f) avoids treating a tradition as uniform. Revise any sentence that lacks evidence or uses “all” without proof.

#### Independent practice — 20 questions for this guide

1. What does the NYSED date range for Standard 6.4 describe? Does it mean the traditions ended around 630 C.E.?
2. Name two locations in the comparison table that students should find on an Eastern Hemisphere map.
3. Why is “founder, if any” a careful question for this unit?
4. Which tradition in the table is connected to Kongzi, also called Confucius? Give the traditional dates listed for his life.
5. Name one text example in the Hindu traditions row. Is that the only important Hindu text?
6. What does the table say about the origin of Hindu traditions and a single founding date?
7. Which central teacher is associated with Buddhism's beginnings in the table? What caution does the table give about dates?
8. According to the Met caption, what moment does the Nalanda Buddha sculpture show?
9. What did the Met say the Torah finials were used to adorn?
10. What does the Met say the sixth-century Syrian cross was used for? Give one limit of that evidence.
11. What are two details a reader could observe in an image before reading its caption?
12. Why can the Chinese Qur'an manuscript not be used to claim that every Qur'an looks the same?
13. What does the Met identify as the material/format of the *Life of Confucius* object? Why is it not evidence from Confucius's own lifetime?
14. A student writes, “All Buddhists use this exact statue.” What is wrong with that claim, and how could it be rewritten?
15. Why should a writer name a place, time, and group when describing a religious practice?
16. Give one difference between a visible image detail and a fact supplied by the museum caption.
17. A student says, “The object proves what all members of the religion believe.” What extra reasoning step is missing?
18. Choose two traditions and name one comparison question that could be answered with the sources in this week.
19. Write one careful similarity or difference sentence supported by two sources. Name both sources.
20. Write a two-sentence answer explaining how a belief system may affect social order or gender roles. What kind of evidence would be needed to support it?

#### Sources and visual credits

- [NYCDOE Passport Grade 6 Unit 3: Comparative World Religions](https://www.weteachnyc.org/resources/resource/passport-social-studies-grade-6-unit-3/) — public unit description, topics, and source/image-based approach; full teacher pack requires NYC DOE access.
- [New York State K–8 Social Studies Framework](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/standards-instruction/ss-framework-k-8a2.pdf), Grade 6 Standard 6.4 — learning expectations and historical frame.
- [Harvard Religion and Public Life: Religion in Context](https://rpl.hds.harvard.edu/religion-context), [Core Principles](https://rpl.hds.harvard.edu/what-we-do/our-approach/core-principles), and [introductory profiles](https://rpl.hds.harvard.edu/HarvardXResourceLibrary) — nondevotional approach, diversity, change over time, and introductory profiles.
- [Harvard RPL, “The Ordination of Nuns in Sri Lanka”](https://rpl.hds.harvard.edu/religion-context/case-studies/gender/ordination-nuns-sri-lanka) — a specific historical case with multiple viewpoints on women's ordination and authority; use its place and time limits.
- [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/confucius/) — Confucius's traditional dates and the layered history of texts and interpretations associated with his name.
- [Wikimedia Commons, “BlankMap-Equirectangular.svg”](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BlankMap-Equirectangular.svg) — modern country outlines drawn from Natural Earth data, dedicated under CC0; use only for broad location practice.
- The six image links above go to Met collection records. The image files are returned by the Met Open Access API; each API record marks its image as public domain: [Torah finials](https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1/objects/903518), [processional cross](https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1/objects/468349), [Shiva Nataraja](https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1/objects/39329), [Nalanda Buddha](https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1/objects/38122), [Qur'an section](https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1/objects/890784), and [*Life of Confucius*](https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1/objects/60773).

**Image-generation need:** None for this week. Use the six authentic Met collection images and the Natural Earth-based map above. Do not generate a map or a generic image that stands in for an entire living tradition.

#### Checked answers and response checks

1. It describes the historical study window NYSED assigns to this comparison; it does not mean any tradition ended around 630 C.E. The traditions continued and changed.
2. Any two correctly located examples from the notes, such as South Asia, the Levant, China, Roman Judea, or Arabia. Check the student's map labels against an atlas.
3. Traditions do not all begin with one named person. Some developed over long periods, and later people shaped them; the question leaves room for that.
4. Confucian traditions; Confucius/Kongzi traditionally lived from 551 to 479 B.C.E. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/confucius/).
5. Examples include the *Bhagavad Gita*, Vedas, or Upanishads. No: the row says these are examples among many important texts.
6. They developed over a long period in South Asia, so the table gives no single founding date for all Hindu traditions.
7. Siddhartha Gautama, remembered as the Buddha; exact dates of his life are debated by scholars.
8. The moment of enlightenment, represented by the Buddha touching the earth. The answer should match the Met's caption for this specific sculpture.
9. They were used on the staves holding a Torah scroll. The caption concerns this object and its cataloged use.
10. It was carried in church processions; the Met also says monumental crosses were mounted in churches in Syria. This one object cannot establish how every Christian community used crosses.
11. Any two visible features the student can point to, such as shape, material, writing, color, or position. They must be visible in the chosen image.
12. It is one manuscript from China dated to the 17th–18th century. A single example cannot represent all copies, regions, periods, or Muslim communities.
13. The Met catalogs four volumes of woodblock-printed books from China, probably late Qing dynasty (1644–1911). That is many centuries after Confucius's traditional lifetime, and the image is a later work about him.
14. The student makes a universal claim from one object. Rewrite: “This Met sculpture from Nalanda shows one historical Buddhist image of the Buddha touching the earth.”
15. Meaning and practice depend on context; communities change over time and differ within traditions. Place, time, and group make the claim checkable and prevent false generalizations.
16. An image detail is directly visible (for example, the cross is silver-colored and has arms); a caption fact comes from the catalog (for example, the Met dates this processional cross to the sixth century and places it in Syria). Accept only details that match the selected image/page.
17. The writer must connect the source to a limited claim and explain its limits. A museum object alone cannot prove a belief shared by every member of a tradition.
18. Accept focused questions that fit sources, such as “How do the two Met pages describe what these objects were used for?” or “How do two traditions preserve or study texts?” The answer must cite the selected sources and stay within their evidence.
19. Answers vary. Check that the sentence is accurate, names two distinct sources, makes an actual comparison, and does not make a universal claim. Examples: the Torah finials and Qur'an manuscript are both text-related objects, but the Met describes different materials, places, dates, and uses; or the Nalanda sculpture and Tamil Nadu Shiva image are both religious artworks but depict different figures and come from different places and times.
20. Answers vary. The student must state a specific, limited example and identify needed evidence, such as a dated law, community account, historical record, or carefully contextualized testimony. One image or one quotation is not enough to support a claim about all members.

Social Studies.title: Social studies week: Han China and Rome — power, work, and “Golden Age” claims
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.contentMarkdown:
**Course link and limits:** NYC Passport Grade 6 Unit 4 is titled **Comparative Classical Civilizations in the Eastern Hemisphere**. Its public overview says students examine the idea of a Golden Age, the role of geography in classical China, Greece, and Rome, lasting contributions, new historical evidence, and significant individuals. It describes a final evidence-based seminar about whether a civilization can be called a Golden Age. This week is one focused comparison of Han China and Rome under Augustus; it is not the full Unit 4 or the full NYSED comparison. Athens, Sparta, the Roman Republic, and other Han periods need separate source studies. Ditmas J.H.S. 62 has not published its current Grade 6 calendar. [NYC Passport Grade 6 Unit 4 overview](https://www.weteachnyc.org/resources/resource/passport-social-studies-grade-6-unit-3-3a88326e-1136-4d37-b099-eca8b645dd01-copy/).

**State scope:** NYSED Standard **6.5, Comparative Classical Civilizations in the Eastern Hemisphere (ca. 600 B.C.E.–ca. 500 C.E.)**, asks students to map classical civilizations and compare Chinese Qin/Han and Greco-Roman societies through religion, work, cities, government, writing/records, technology, and social hierarchy. It asks students to examine political systems and decide whether evidence supports a “Golden Age” claim. The standard's broad period is not one unbroken age of peace. [New York State K–8 Social Studies Framework, Grade 6, Standard 6.5](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/standards-instruction/ss-framework-k-8a2.pdf); [NYSED standard detail](https://nylearns.org/module/standards/Tools/StandardDetail?LinkStandardId=0&StandardId=189312).

**Question for the week:** What can real objects and records tell us about authority, work, and public life in Han China and Roman society? Do they prove that either society was a “Golden Age” for everyone?

#### Read this first: a source can show one part of the past

The Han dynasty ruled in China from the late third century B.C.E. into the third century C.E. The Met dates the Han objects used below to the Eastern Han period (25–220 C.E.). Rome's Republic came before the imperial period. The Met's Augustus source says Augustus ruled from 27 B.C.E. to 14 C.E.; it dates the surviving portrait fragment to about 14–37 C.E., during the rule of his successor Tiberius. Those dates overlap the Han period, but the two empires were not identical in size, government, or daily life. [World History Encyclopedia, “Han Dynasty”](https://www.worldhistory.org/Han_Dynasty/); [The Met, “Marble portrait of the emperor Augustus”](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/247993).

For Han China, we will use a carved tomb panel and small models that the museum catalogs as tomb pottery. A tomb object is evidence of what someone chose to place in a burial setting. It is not a census of every home, farm, or belief. For Rome, we will read the Met's account of an official portrait and a passage from Augustus's own record, the *Res Gestae*. A ruler's own record is a valuable primary source for what he wanted to claim; it is not a neutral account of every person's life.

The Unit 4 overview describes a Golden Age as a period of peace, prosperity, and cultural achievement. To judge that claim, ask: **Which years? Which people benefited? What evidence shows peace or prosperity? What evidence shows achievements? Who is missing from the source?** A beautiful object or strong ruler is not enough by itself to prove that a whole society was peaceful or fair.

#### Key words in simple English

- **Dynasty**: a line of rulers, often connected by family or succession.
- **Empire**: a state that controls a large area and many peoples.
- **Imperial**: connected to an emperor or an empire.
- **Relief**: a picture carved so some parts stand out from a flat surface.
- **Tomb pottery/model**: a pottery object the museum identifies as connected with a tomb; it may be a model of a real object.
- **Idealized**: shown in a way that emphasizes desired qualities rather than ordinary age or appearance.
- **Primary source**: a record or object made in the time being studied, or by a person involved in it.
- **Aqueduct**: a built channel or bridge that carries water toward a town or city.
- **Prosperity**: a period when people or a society have resources and economic well-being; evidence must show who had them.
- **Inference**: an idea drawn from evidence; label it so it is not mistaken for a fact stated by the source.

#### Source reading: two societies, four real objects, and one ruler's record

**Han China — a court in a tomb relief.** The Met dates this limestone panel to the early second century, during the Eastern Han. Its caption identifies the large figure at the left as Xiwangmu, the Queen Mother of the West, and says she played a major role in Han funerary beliefs. The Met explains that the ordered arrangement of Xiwangmu and attendants resembles Han images of heavenly courts; under Confucian influence, those heavenly courts began to parallel the organization of earthly courts. This is a museum interpretation of one object. It can support a claim about how this panel shows order and belief; it cannot show that every Han person held the same belief or lived under identical conditions. [The Met, “Tomb Panel with Relief of Figures in a Pavilion”](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/44791).

**Han China — work and water in tomb models.** The Met catalogs an Eastern Han **Model of Mill** and a **Model of Wellhead with Bucket** as pottery objects. Their titles and forms give students visible evidence of tools connected with grinding and drawing water. The museum records them as objects, not as a count of how often these tools were used. A careful claim is “Han tomb pottery includes a model of a mill,” not “every Han family owned a mill.” The same caution applies to the well model. [The Met, “Model of Mill”](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/44430); [The Met, “Model of Wellhead with Bucket”](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/49532).

**Rome — an emperor's public image.** The Met dates its marble portrait of Augustus to about 14–37 C.E. The museum says the fragment may have belonged to a seated statue made during the reign of Tiberius, Augustus's successor. Its audio account says hundreds of official portraits of Augustus were distributed through the empire. It describes Augustus as individualized but idealized and ageless. The Met calls this kind of ruler image an important tool of propaganda: it was made to spread a message about the ruler. That is a useful source clue, not proof that every viewer believed the message. [The Met, “Marble portrait of the emperor Augustus” and its audio transcript](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/247993).

**Rome — Augustus describes his honors.** The Met transcript identifies a short passage from Augustus's *Res Gestae* 34. In it, Augustus says that the Senate and Roman people honored him with a golden shield for qualities including bravery, justice, and piety. He also says the Senate formally gave him the name Augustus. These are claims in a record written from Augustus's point of view. They show how he described his authority and honors; compare them with the portrait and ask whose voices the record does not include.

**Roman engineering — water at Segovia.** The Roman aqueduct at Segovia, in modern Spain, is a real structure that carried water toward a city. UNESCO describes the visible monument as 813 meters long, with two levels of arches and 128 pillars. Segovia's official tourism source says the exact construction date is unknown and places it after 112 C.E.; UNESCO's overview gives a different approximate date. For this week, use the safe shared fact—this is Roman engineering—and do not memorize one exact construction year. The difference between sources is a reason to check dates before repeating them. [UNESCO World Heritage Centre, “Old Town of Segovia and its Aqueduct”](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/311); [Segovia official tourism, aqueduct features and date](https://turismodesegovia.com/en/aqueduct/features-and-interesting-facts).

#### Visual sources: look, read, and mark the limit

**Map:** Mark China, the Mediterranean Sea, Italy/Rome, and Segovia in modern Spain on this blank world map. Its borders are modern, not Han or Roman borders. Add a small label “present-day boundaries” so no one reads them as ancient borders. [Wikimedia Commons map record and CC0 dedication](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BlankMap-Equirectangular.svg).

![Blank world map with modern country outlines, based on Natural Earth data.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/BlankMap-Equirectangular.svg/1920px-BlankMap-Equirectangular.svg.png)

**Han tomb panel:** Look for differences in size and position. Then compare your observation with the Met caption's identification of Xiwangmu and attendants.

![Han limestone tomb panel showing figures arranged in a pavilion.](https://images.metmuseum.org/CRDImages/as/web-large/DT5067.jpg)

**Han work models:** Compare the pictured shapes with the Met titles. Do not claim how common a tool was from one burial object.

![Eastern Han pottery model of a mill in The Met collection.](https://images.metmuseum.org/CRDImages/as/web-large/1994_605_134_L36670.jpg)

![Eastern Han pottery model of a wellhead with bucket in The Met collection.](https://images.metmuseum.org/CRDImages/as/web-large/2000_662_12ab_L35951.JPG)

**Roman ruler portrait:** Notice what the sculptor made visible about the ruler, then read the Met caption about an idealized public image.

![Marble portrait fragment of the Roman emperor Augustus.](https://images.metmuseum.org/CRDImages/gr/web-large/DP337220.jpg)

**Roman aqueduct:** This current photograph shows the surviving ancient structure in its modern city setting; the image is not an ancient photograph. Photo by Manuel González Olaechea y Franco, [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:AcueductoSegovia04.JPG).

![The surviving Roman aqueduct at Segovia, Spain.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/AcueductoSegovia04.JPG/1280px-AcueductoSegovia04.JPG)

#### Five study sessions — 50–60 minutes each

| Day | Focus and steps | Work to save |
|---|---|---|
| **1 — Locate and set the time** | 10 min: read the NYSED Standard 6.5 scope note. 15 min: mark China, Rome, Segovia, and the Mediterranean on the map. 15 min: make a timeline for the Han period and Augustus's rule; mark which dates overlap. 10 min: read the Golden Age questions. 5 min: exit ticket. | Map and timeline with date sources; one sentence explaining that modern borders on the map are not ancient borders. |
| **2 — Read Han evidence** | 10 min: inspect the tomb panel silently. 15 min: read its Met caption and paraphrase the museum's interpretation. 15 min: inspect the mill and wellhead models and read their object labels. 10 min: write an observation, a caption fact, and a question for each. 5 min: exit ticket. | Three source cards: tomb panel, mill model, wellhead model. Keep “I see,” “the museum says,” and “I infer” in separate columns. |
| **3 — Read Roman evidence** | 10 min: inspect Augustus's portrait. 15 min: read the Met account and identify its evidence for idealization and distribution. 15 min: summarize the *Res Gestae* claims in your own words. 10 min: read the Segovia source and note its measurements plus date uncertainty. 5 min: exit ticket. | Two evidence cards: ruler portrait/record and aqueduct. Include one source limit for each. |
| **4 — Compare and test claims** | 10 min: fill the comparison chart below. 15 min: compare imperial authority and court imagery. 15 min: compare what the work models and aqueduct show about tools, water, or engineering. 10 min: mark each statement as source fact, inference, or unsupported generalization. 5 min: revise one sentence. | Completed comparison chart with at least four rows and source names in each row. |
| **5 — Golden Age seminar and writing** | 8 min: read the success criteria. 12 min: choose a claim and collect one Han and one Roman detail. 15 min: discuss whether your evidence supports a limited Golden Age claim. 15 min: write a short response. 5 min: self-check. | A claim paragraph plus a note naming what the sources cannot establish. |

**Comparison chart:** Use these rows: (1) authority/rulers; (2) city, water, and geography; (3) work or technology; (4) belief and social order; (5) who appears in the evidence; (6) what still needs a source. An acceptable chart can say “not enough evidence yet.” Do not fill gaps from memory and label them source facts.

**Writing frame:** “For [named place and period], the evidence [supports / partly supports / does not yet prove] a Golden Age claim because ____. The Han source shows ____, according to ____. The Roman source shows ____, according to ____. A similarity/difference is ____. These sources do not tell us ____, so the claim should remain limited to ____.”

**End-of-week check:** A strong answer uses one accurate detail from a Han source and one from a Roman source; distinguishes the Augustus record from a neutral account; distinguishes an artifact from a museum's interpretation; names the date/place; explains one similarity or difference; and says what evidence is still missing before making a claim about prosperity or life for all people.

#### Independent practice — 20 questions for this guide

1. What is the title of NYC Passport Grade 6 Unit 4?
2. What broad date range does NYSED Standard 6.5 use?
3. Name the three kinds of evidence named in the unit's Golden Age idea.
4. Which two civilizations are compared in this focused week? What important limitation does that create?
5. The Met dates the Han tomb panel to the early second century. Which dynasty period does the record name?
6. Whom does the Met identify as the large figure at the left of the Han relief?
7. What does the Met say about the ordered heavenly court and earthly court in later Han representations?
8. Why can one tomb panel not prove that every Han person shared one belief?
9. What are the titles of the two Han work-related models used here?
10. Give one safe claim supported by the model labels and one claim they do not prove.
11. What years does the Met give for Augustus's rule, and what date range does it give for the portrait fragment?
12. What does the Met say about the distribution and style of Augustus's official portraits?
13. What did Augustus's *Res Gestae* say about the golden shield? Why should we treat that account as a point of view?
14. What does the portrait show directly, and what does the Met interpretation add?
15. Where is Segovia, and what water structure is the UNESCO source describing?
16. Name two measurements in UNESCO's description of the aqueduct.
17. Why does this guide avoid giving one exact year for the aqueduct's construction?
18. Give one Han/Rome similarity and cite one source for each side.
19. Write one evidence-based reason for or against calling one of these periods a Golden Age. Name one kind of evidence still needed.
20. A student writes, “The Han and Roman Empires were Golden Ages for everyone because they had art and engineering.” Identify two problems and revise it into a limited claim.

#### Sources and image credits

- [NYC Passport Grade 6 Unit 4 overview](https://www.weteachnyc.org/resources/resource/passport-social-studies-grade-6-unit-3-3a88326e-1136-4d37-b099-eca8b645dd01-copy/) — actual public unit title, topics, Golden Age question, and source-based project; the full teacher pack is login-gated.
- [New York State K–8 Social Studies Framework](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/standards-instruction/ss-framework-k-8a2.pdf), Grade 6 Standard 6.5 — comparison requirements and historical frame.
- [World History Encyclopedia, “Han Dynasty”](https://www.worldhistory.org/Han_Dynasty/) — supplemental dynasty background; the lessons rely on the specific museum records for object facts.
- [The Met, Han tomb panel](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/44791), [Model of Mill](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/44430), and [Model of Wellhead with Bucket](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/49532) — captions, dates, object types, and visual evidence. The Met's Open Access API marks these image files public domain.
- [The Met, Augustus portrait and audio transcript](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/247993) — object date, the museum's interpretation, and the excerpt it identifies as *Res Gestae* 34. The transcript is used here as a paraphrased primary-source example.
- [UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Segovia](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/311) and [Segovia official tourism, aqueduct features](https://turismodesegovia.com/en/aqueduct/features-and-interesting-facts) — structure, measurements, location, and the uncertainty around its exact date.
- [Wikimedia Commons, map record](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BlankMap-Equirectangular.svg) — present-day outline map based on Natural Earth data, CC0. [Aqueduct photograph](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:AcueductoSegovia04.JPG) by Manuel González Olaechea y Franco, CC BY-SA 3.0.

**Image-generation need:** None for this focused week. It uses a sourced outline map, four public-domain Met collection images, and a credited current photo of the Roman aqueduct. No AI-generated map or invented historical image is needed.

Social Studies.title: Social studies week: Sogdian merchants and the Silk Roads — routes, goods, and disruption
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.contentMarkdown:
**Course link and limits:** NYC Passport Grade 6 Unit 5 is **The Mediterranean World and Interactions Across the Eastern Hemisphere**. Its public overview includes the Silk Road, Byzantine and Islamic history, Islamic caliphates, and travelers such as Mansa Musa, Ibn Battuta, Marco Polo, and Zheng He. It asks students to research an interaction and create a map with captions and illustrations. This week focuses on one well-documented example: Sogdian merchants and the overland networks across Central Asia. It does not cover every Unit 5 topic or confirm Ditmas J.H.S. 62's class schedule. [NYC Passport Grade 6 Unit 5 overview](https://www.weteachnyc.org/resources/resource/passport-social-studies-grade-6-unit-3-236c3902-9461-4bac-a589-73875d790855-copy/); [NYC Social Studies & Civics Hub, Grade 6](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/middle/6th-grade).

**State scope:** NYSED Standard **6.7, Interactions Across the Eastern Hemisphere**, asks students to study the Silk Roads, Indian Ocean routes, and Trans-Saharan routes as networks that connected regions. It also names travelers who crossed regions, including Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta, Mansa Musa, and Zheng He. This week follows the Silk Roads part only; other routes and travelers need their own studies. [New York State K–8 Social Studies Framework, Grade 6, Standard 6.7](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/curriculum-instruction/ss-framework-k-8a2.pdf).

#### Read this first: the Silk Roads were a network

The phrase **Silk Road** can make it sound like one road that ran from China to Europe. UNESCO explains that merchants used many connected land and sea routes, and travelers often covered one part, sold or exchanged goods at a city, then continued by another route. Routes shifted over time as leaders, conflicts, rivers, and trading needs changed. The network carried silk, but it also carried other goods, people, skills, languages, religions, and ideas. “Silk Roads” is a useful name for the connected routes; it was not the name that ancient merchants used. [UNESCO, “About the Silk Roads”](https://www.unesco.org/en/silk-roads/about-silk-roads?hub=196704); [British Museum, “Silk Roads”](https://www.britishmuseum.org/exhibitions/silk-roads).

One group of merchants in this history were the Sogdians, people from Central Asia near Samarkand in what is now southern Uzbekistan and western Tajikistan. They traveled and traded across Eurasia. The British Museum describes Sogdians as merchants, travelers, diplomats, artists, and storytellers. They also helped carry religious texts and ideas between communities. These roles come from historical research; the Sogdians were not the only people who used the routes. [British Museum, “Who were the Sogdians?”](https://www.britishmuseum.org/blog/who-were-sogdians); [University of Washington, “The Sogdian Ancient Letters”](https://depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/sogdlet.html).

#### A real letter from the network — written around 313 C.E.

The Sogdian Ancient Letters were written on paper by merchants and family members in western China around the early fourth century. Scholars place one likely date at 312 or 313 C.E.; the exact dating has been debated. Archaeologist Aurel Stein found the letters in 1907 at a watchtower west of Dunhuang, in present-day Gansu, China. Researchers think they may have been in a mailbag that was lost or taken by a Chinese garrison while it was being carried. The originals are held by the British Library. The Smithsonian's Sogdians project provides a photograph and background; the University of Washington page provides a translation by Nicholas Sims-Williams with an introduction by Daniel C. Waugh. [Smithsonian, “Ancient Letters”](https://sogdians.si.edu/ancient-letters/); [University of Washington translation and notes](https://depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/sogdlet.html).

**Letter 2** was sent by Nanai-vandak to Varzakk in Samarkand. The translator's introduction says the writer was likely in Jincheng, now Lanzhou, and writing to a business contact at home. In the letter, the writer says he has gone years without news from some Sogdians traveling in China. He reports destruction and famine affecting cities and travelers. The letter also discusses the sale of cloth, money held on deposit, and the division of money or goods among named people. The translation has gaps and uncertain words, so readers should not treat every damaged line as exact.

This letter shows that long-distance trade depended on communication and relationships across cities, and that war and hunger could disrupt those ties. That is a limited inference from one letter. It does not tell us that every merchant had the same experience, that all trade stopped, or that all travelers were Sogdian. [University of Washington, “The Sogdian Ancient Letters,” introduction and Letter 2](https://depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/sogdlet.html).

UNESCO describes the routes as carrying far more than silk. Its examples include textiles, spices, grains, fruits, tools, metal objects, religious items, art, and precious stones. UNESCO also explains that cities along the routes became places where travelers traded and shared knowledge, languages, crafts, and beliefs. The Sogdian letter gives a close view of one merchant's problems; UNESCO provides a broad overview of the longer networks. These sources answer different questions.

#### Key words in simple English

- **Network**: several connected routes or places, not just one road.
- **Merchant**: a person who buys, sells, or trades goods.
- **Caravan**: a group of travelers moving together, often with pack animals and goods.
- **Overland / maritime**: travel by land / travel by sea.
- **Sogdian**: a person, language, or culture connected with Sogdiana, a region near present-day Samarkand.
- **Deposit**: money or property left with another person or place for safekeeping.
- **Primary source**: an object or record from the time being studied, such as a letter written by someone who lived then.
- **Translation**: writing the meaning of a text in another language; some words can be uncertain.
- **Inference**: a conclusion based on clues. Label it so it is not confused with what a source states.

#### Visual source: map the route as a set of links

Use this modern outline map to mark **Samarkand**, **Jincheng/Lanzhou**, **Dunhuang**, and **Luoyang**. Place each point approximately and label present-day countries. Then draw at least two possible route segments; do not draw one unbroken “Silk Road” line. The locations come from the letter's introduction and the Smithsonian source page. The map's borders are modern and are not the borders of ancient states. For a source map that shows many land and sea paths, open UNESCO's Silk Roads map on its program page. [Wikimedia Commons map record and CC0 dedication](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BlankMap-Equirectangular.svg); [UNESCO Silk Roads map and overview](https://www.unesco.org/en/silk-roads/about-silk-roads?hub=196704).

![Blank world map with present-day country outlines, based on Natural Earth data.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/BlankMap-Equirectangular.svg/1920px-BlankMap-Equirectangular.svg.png)

**Manuscript image:** Open the Smithsonian's [Ancient Letters page](https://sogdians.si.edu/ancient-letters/) to view the British Library photograph of Sogdian Letters 1 and 2. The page credits the photograph to the British Library Board. This guide links to it instead of copying the image file.

#### Five study sessions — 50–60 minutes each

| Day | Focus and steps | Work to save |
|---|---|---|
| **1 — Put the network on a map** | 10 min: read the opening section. 15 min: locate Samarkand, Jincheng/Lanzhou, Dunhuang, and Luoyang. 15 min: read UNESCO's description of land and sea routes. 10 min: draw multiple possible route segments and explain why the map does not show one ancient road. 5 min: exit ticket. | Annotated map, source names, and a note that modern borders are not ancient boundaries. |
| **2 — Meet the Sogdian merchants** | 10 min: read the British Museum's Sogdian overview. 15 min: make a people/place/time card from the source. 15 min: list roles the source supports (merchant, traveler, diplomat, artist, translator) and one example for each that the page actually gives. 10 min: write one question that the source cannot answer. 5 min: exit ticket. | A people/place/time card and a fact-versus-question chart. |
| **3 — Read Letter 2 as evidence** | 10 min: open the University of Washington translation; note the author, addressee, and date caveat. 15 min: read the teacher-friendly paraphrase above, then examine the translated letter. 15 min: highlight lines about travel/news, trade goods, and money. 10 min: record one fact, one inference, and one uncertainty. 5 min: exit ticket. | A source card naming Letter 2 and its translator, with fact/inference/uncertainty columns. Do not copy a long passage. |
| **4 — Trace goods and effects** | 10 min: compare the letter's named commodities with UNESCO's broader list. 15 min: choose one item (such as silk, pepper, cloth, or musk) and trace only the movements the sources support. 15 min: make a cause/effect chain for how conflict or lost contact could disrupt a trade relationship. 10 min: add one limit to the chain. 5 min: exit ticket. | A trade chain with a source beside every step; label any unsourced step as a question, not a fact. |
| **5 — Create a source-based route story** | 8 min: choose one interaction (a letter, good, idea, or person). 12 min: plan a map caption with two place names and two source facts. 20 min: write the claim paragraph below. 10 min: revise for route accuracy and source limits. 5 min: self-check. | A map with a caption and a short claim supported by two sources. |

**Writing frame:** “The Silk Roads were a network rather than one road. In this case, [source/person/good] connected [place] and [place]. The [primary source / museum or UNESCO account] says ____. This supports the claim that ____. It does not prove ____. One limit is ____.”

**End-of-week check:** A strong response uses the map to show multiple routes, correctly names the Sogdian letter's author or addressee, uses one detail from the letter and one from a secondary source, marks uncertain translation or dating, and does not claim that every Silk Road traveler or merchant was Sogdian.

#### Independent practice — 20 questions for this guide

1. What is the title of NYC Passport Grade 6 Unit 5?
2. Why does UNESCO describe the Silk Roads as a network instead of one road?
3. What modern region was near the Sogdian homeland around Samarkand?
4. Name two different roles the British Museum says Sogdians had.
5. Where and when were the Sogdian Ancient Letters found?
6. What material were the ancient letters written on?
7. Who sent Letter 2, and to whom was it addressed?
8. About when was Letter 2 written? Why should a student avoid giving a more exact date as certain?
9. Name two goods mentioned in the introduction to the letters.
10. What does Letter 2 report about communication with Sogdians traveling inside China?
11. What does Letter 2 tell us about one danger to travel or trade at that time?
12. How does the letter show that trade involved more than moving an object from one city to another?
13. What can the letter not prove about all Silk Road merchants?
14. According to UNESCO, name two goods besides silk that moved along these networks.
15. What else besides goods could move along the routes?
16. What are two limits of the modern outline map used in the lesson?
17. Why should a map show route segments rather than one single line?
18. Sort this statement: “The letter says a merchant used money held on deposit.” Is it a source fact, inference, or unsupported generalization?
19. Write a one-sentence claim about one way conflict affected trade, using a detail from Letter 2.
20. Write a three-sentence map caption using two locations, one fact from the letter, one fact from UNESCO or the British Museum, and one source limit.

#### Sources and visual credits

- [NYC Passport Grade 6 Unit 5 overview](https://www.weteachnyc.org/resources/resource/passport-social-studies-grade-6-unit-3-236c3902-9461-4bac-a589-73875d790855-copy/) — published title, topic examples, source analysis, and map/caption project; full teacher materials may require NYC DOE access.

- [UNESCO, “About the Silk Roads”](https://www.unesco.org/en/silk-roads/about-silk-roads?hub=196704) — network, goods, sea links, cultural exchange, and route variation.
- [British Museum, “Who were the Sogdians?”](https://www.britishmuseum.org/blog/who-were-sogdians) — people, homeland, merchant roles, and exchanges.
- [Smithsonian, “Ancient Letters”](https://sogdians.si.edu/ancient-letters/) — manuscript photo and context; the page credits the photograph to the British Library Board, so this guide links to the image rather than reproducing it.
- [University of Washington, “The Sogdian Ancient Letters”](https://depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/sogdlet.html) — historical introduction and Letter 2 translation by Nicholas Sims-Williams. The guide paraphrases the translation and does not reprint it.
- [Wikimedia Commons blank map](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BlankMap-Equirectangular.svg) — Natural Earth base map dedicated under CC0; modern borders only.

**Image-generation need:** None for this week. Use the licensed blank map, UNESCO's linked route map, and the Smithsonian manuscript page. The manuscript photograph is linked for on-page study because it is credited to the British Library; do not download or copy it into the website without permission.

Science.title: Science week: cells as working systems
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
**Scope label:** New York places these expectations in the **Grades 6–8 band**. The standards require evidence that living things are made of one or more cells (MS-LS1-1) and a model linking a cell's parts to the work of the whole cell (MS-LS1-2). They name the nucleus, chloroplasts, mitochondria, cell membrane, and cell wall. The assessment boundary says students are not expected to learn detailed chemistry of each part; detailed structure/function links are limited to the membrane and wall. This is state scope, not proof that Ditmas teaches this unit in Grade 6. [NYS P–12 Science Learning Standards, MS-LS1-1 and MS-LS1-2](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/curriculum-instruction/p-12-science-learning-standards.pdf); [Ditmas science department page](https://sites.google.com/iditmas.org/ditmas-j-h-s-62/ditmas-staff/science-department) identifies the department but does not publish its current unit calendar.

**Source reading (student-friendly paraphrase, not a school-book passage):**

A cell is the smallest unit that is alive. Some living things are one cell. Other living things are made of many cells. In a cell, different parts do different jobs, and the parts work together. The cell membrane is the cell's boundary. It controls what enters and leaves. A cell wall is a stronger outside layer found in plant cells. The nucleus contains DNA, which carries genetic information. Mitochondria help cells use energy from food by making a molecule called ATP. Plant cells also have chloroplasts. New York's standard asks students to connect these parts to the cell as a whole, not to memorize detailed chemical steps. A diagram is a model: it can show names, locations, and relationships, but it cannot show every detail of a real cell. Cell shapes and sizes vary. [NYSED science standards, MS-LS1-1/2 and LS1.A](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/curriculum-instruction/p-12-science-learning-standards.pdf); [National Institute of General Medical Sciences, “Take a Tour of Your Cells’ Organelles!”](https://www.nigms.nih.gov/biobeat/2021/03/take-a-tour-of-your-cells-organelles) (archived explainer; its scale drawings are models, not photographs).

**Key words:**

- **cell:** the smallest unit that can be alive.
- **cell membrane:** the boundary that controls what enters and leaves a cell.
- **cell wall:** a stiff outer layer around plant cells.
- **nucleus:** a cell part that contains most of the cell's DNA.
- **DNA:** information used by living things and their cells.
- **mitochondrion / mitochondria:** a cell structure / cell structures that help turn energy from food into ATP the cell can use.
- **chloroplast:** a structure found in plant cells; the NYS standard asks students to relate it to the whole cell.
- **model:** a simplified representation used to show or test an idea.

**Five sessions, 50–60 minutes each:**

| Day | Work and evidence to save |
|---|---|
| 1 — Read and sort claims | Read the source reading twice. Highlight what the NYSED standard says, circle facts supported by the NIH explainer, and put a star beside a model limitation. Sort six cards into “one cell,” “many cells,” or “the source does not say.” For the last group, record which source you would need. |
| 2 — Boundaries and movement | On a blank cell outline, draw the membrane and wall as separate layers. Add three arrows entering and two leaving. Write a caption explaining which part controls movement. Do not claim that the wall and membrane do the same job. Check the caption against MS-LS1-2. |
| 3 — Parts support the whole | Build a function map: food energy → mitochondria help make ATP → the cell uses energy to function. Add nucleus/DNA, membrane, wall, and chloroplast around the map. For each arrow, write whether the source supports it directly or whether the diagram is only showing a relationship named by the standard. |
| 4 — Test a model | Use the supplied/generated cell diagram. Check every label against the key words and cited sources. Write three things the model shows well and three limits. Required limits: it is not to scale; it does not show every cell part or process; a drawing cannot prove that every cell has the same shape. Correct any label that claims an animal cell has a plant cell wall or chloroplast. |
| 5 — Explain from evidence | Write a short answer to: “How do parts help a cell work as a whole?” Include the membrane, one other named part, a source clue for each, and one model limit. Then complete the independent check below without looking at notes. |

**Independent check — supplemental practice, not a school or NYSED test:**

1. What is the smallest unit that can be alive?
2. Does every organism have many cells? Give the source-supported answer.
3. Which part controls what enters and leaves a cell?
4. What is one difference between a cell wall and a cell membrane?
5. What information does the nucleus contain?
6. What do mitochondria help a cell make from energy in food?
7. Which two plant-cell parts are named in the NYS standard besides the cell membrane and nucleus?
8. A drawing makes the nucleus the size of a basketball and the rest of the cell the size of a classroom. Can that drawing prove real relative sizes? Explain.
9. A student writes, “The cell wall controls everything that enters and leaves.” Which source fact corrects the claim?
10. Name two things a cell model can show and two things it cannot show.
11. A source says a cell part has a named role. Does that prove the exact same shape and size for that part in every cell? Explain.
12. Write a four-sentence explanation of how two cell parts support the cell as a whole. Put a source clue in parentheses after each fact.

**Checked answers:** 1) A cell. 2) No; some living things consist of one cell, while others consist of many. 3) Cell membrane. 4) The membrane controls what enters/leaves; the wall is a stronger outside layer around plant cells. 5) DNA/genetic information. 6) ATP, a form the cell can use. 7) Chloroplasts and cell walls. 8) No; a model may change size to make parts visible, so its key or caption must state that it is not to scale. 9) The NYS standard says the membrane controls what enters/leaves; it does not give that job to the wall. 10) It can show labels, boundaries, or relationships; it cannot show every tiny detail, every chemical process, or prove all cells look alike. 11) No; the standard gives functions and the NIGMS page gives examples and typical sizes, but neither says every cell has an identical shape and size. 12) Check that both parts are named accurately, the roles match the two cited sources, the explanation connects them to the whole cell, and the source clues identify the supporting standard or NIGMS explanation. Different clear wording is acceptable.

**Visual:** The diagram below is a simplified model, not to scale. It includes a nucleus, mitochondria, and plant-only structures in the plant cell; the page leaves space for students to add labels. Cells vary in shape and size.

![Unlabeled plant and animal cell models with nucleus and mitochondria in both and cell wall, chloroplasts, and large vacuole in the plant cell](images/grade-06/science/g06-science-cell-comparison.png)

Caption: Left is a plant-cell model; right is an animal-cell model. Both show a nucleus and mitochondria; the plant model also shows a wall, chloroplasts, and a large vacuole. The models are not to scale, and real cells vary.
