Science.title: Science week: balanced forces, motion, and a fair test
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
**Scope note:** This unit supports the New York middle-school science standard MS-PS2-2. The standard is written for Grades 6–8 as a band; it does not establish that Ditmas teaches this topic in Grade 6, uses the activity below, or follows this order. The school-specific science sequence remains unconfirmed. This week's goal is to explain how the combined forces on an object relate to a change in its motion and to plan a test that changes one factor at a time.

**Published sources:** [New York State Middle School Science Learning Standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/standards-instruction/ms-science-learning-standards.pdf), MS-PS2-2; [TeachEngineering, “Exploring Variables While Testing & Improving Mint-Mobiles”](https://www.teachengineering.org/activities/view/cub-2537-exploring-variables-mint-mobiles-middle-school), a published activity tagged Grade 7 (Grades 6–8); and the [student design worksheet](https://teachengwebstorageprod.blob.core.windows.net/te-content-prod/cub-2537-mint-mobiles-middle-design-worksheet.pdf). The published activity asks students to set design goals and limits, choose variables, test a small vehicle, measure how far it travels, predict a later trial, and use evidence to improve the design. Its Figure 3 shows one vehicle with four wheels and a later test with six wheels. Those are source details; no test distances are supplied here because students collect their own data.

#### Learn the ideas

**A force is a push or a pull from one object on another.** A hand can push a cart. A floor can push up on a book. Earth pulls objects toward itself. Friction is a force between touching surfaces that resists sliding; it also affects how wheels grip and roll. A newton (N) is a unit used to measure force. A force arrow in a diagram shows the direction of a force; a longer arrow can stand for a stronger force when the diagram says that arrow length represents strength.

**Add the forces to find the net force.** “Net force” means the combined effect of all the forces on one object. In a one-direction model, right and left forces oppose each other. Equal opposite forces have a net force of zero and are balanced. Unequal opposite forces leave a net force toward the stronger side and are unbalanced. Forces in the same direction add. Always name the object and the direction being described.

**Zero net force does not mean “not moving.”** If a book is resting on a table, the upward support from the table and the downward pull of Earth balance in this simple model; the book stays at rest. If a puck is already sliding straight ahead at a steady speed and the total force on it is zero, it keeps the same motion in the model. In a real room, friction or another force usually changes that motion. A net force changes motion: the object may speed up, slow down, or turn. The net-force direction describes the change in motion, not automatically the direction the object is already traveling. For example, a cart moving left with a net force to the right first slows; it does not instantly start moving right.

**Mass and force both matter.** For the same object, a larger net force causes a larger change in motion. For the same net force, a larger mass has a smaller change in motion. This week uses those comparisons in words and in one-direction arrow models. It does not require students to calculate acceleration with a formula.

**A fair test changes one thing at a time.** The factor you deliberately change is the independent variable. The result you measure is the dependent variable. Conditions kept the same are controls. If a group changes the cart's mass and the ramp height at once, it cannot tell which change affected the travel distance. Repeat each setup so an unusual run does not decide the result. Record actual observations; do not fill a table with invented data.

#### Five-session study plan — about 55–65 minutes each

| Session | Read, investigate, and practice | Evidence to keep |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Name forces and motion | Read the first three idea sections. Study the cart diagram below. For each arrow, name the object receiving the force and the direction. Explain the difference between “the cart is moving right” and “the net force is right.” | A labeled force sketch and a short explanation that separates motion direction from net-force direction. |
| 2 — Compare balanced and unbalanced forces | Use the arrow models in the practice set. Find the combined force in one direction. For a zero-net-force case, decide whether the object is at rest or already moving before predicting its motion. | Completed force tables with direction, balance label, and a sentence about the motion. |
| 3 — Plan the investigation | Read the TeachEngineering activity description and worksheet. Copy its design question in your own words. Choose one factor: for example, the force pulling the same cart or the cart's mass. Name the measurement and every condition to hold steady. | A test plan with a question, prediction, independent variable, dependent variable, controls, tools, and a repeat plan. |
| 4 — Collect evidence | If a toy cart and spring scale are available, test the same cart on the same level surface with several gentle pull strengths, keeping the cart and surface fixed. Use the same start mark and time interval. Run each setting three times. For a mass comparison, use a simulation only if it lets you hold the net force steady while changing mass; otherwise record that the physical trial also changed friction and cannot isolate mass by itself. If materials are unavailable, use the [PhET Forces and Motion: Basics simulation](https://phet.colorado.edu/en/simulations/forces-and-motion-basics) to explore the controls it provides and record the screen setting for each trial. Do not claim a variable was controlled if the tool does not let you hold it steady. | A real data table with units, three trials per setting when possible, and a note about measurement limits. No sample numbers are supplied as if they were observed. |
| 5 — Explain and improve | Compare the repeated trials. Look for a pattern, but say when results are mixed. Write a claim supported by two data details. Then connect the reasoning to the published Mint-Mobile design task: choose one design feature, predict its effect, test it, and use evidence to decide what to change next. | A claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph and a revised vehicle sketch with one evidence-based design change. |

#### Source-based investigation and recorded evidence

The TeachEngineering Mint-Mobile activity is a real published middle-grade design activity, not evidence of Ditmas homework. Its student work asks teams to set criteria such as rolling smoothly, traveling straight, and staying together; list limits such as the available materials and ramp size; select one variable; measure distance traveled; and predict a later run. It lists mass, number of wheels, wheel type, ramp length, and ramp angle as possible variables. Its worksheet expects students to record their own trials.

Use the published source's four-wheel versus six-wheel example to ask: “What must stay the same to test whether wheel count affected this vehicle's travel?” A careful answer holds the same car body, ramp, start point, release method, floor, and measurement method steady. It changes only wheel count between the two planned designs. The source image is a model of a test; it does not prove that six wheels always travel farther. Wheel alignment, friction, and build differences can affect the result, so the students' own repeated measurements are the evidence.

**Guide-designed investigation option (not a published Ditmas lab):** Use a small toy cart, a low-force spring scale, a timer, and tape marks on a level tabletop. For a force test, keep the cart mass, wheels, surface, start place, pull direction, and time interval fixed. Change only the target pull shown on the scale; keep the pull near that target and record the reading if it varies. Measure how far the cart moves during the same time interval. Repeat each setting three times. For a separate mass comparison, use a simulation only if it allows net force and starting conditions to stay fixed while mass changes. On a physical table, the same applied pull does not guarantee the same net force: adding mass can also change friction. If students try that physical comparison, label the conclusion as a result for that setup and name friction as a limit. Use gentle pulls, secure the table area, and stop if the cart reaches an edge. If a spring scale is not available, use the linked simulation and state which settings it actually allows you to control. Do not compare a ramp run with a level-table run as if only mass changed.

**Blank data record:**

| Trial setting | What changed? | What stayed the same? | Run 1 distance | Run 2 distance | Run 3 distance | Pattern or uncertainty |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | | | | | | |
| B | | | | | | |
| C | | | | | | |

#### Practice set — source reading and new guide questions

Questions 1–5 use the source standard and the published Mint-Mobile activity. Questions 6–16 are new practice questions written for this guide; they are not copied from a textbook, state test, or Ditmas lesson.

1. In the Mint-Mobile activity, which measurement is the result students record after a run?
2. The source's Figure 3 compares a four-wheel version and a six-wheel version. Name two conditions that should stay the same for a fair wheel-count comparison.
3. Why does a team make a prediction before its next test rather than after it?
4. A team changes both the ramp angle and the car's mass, then sees a different distance. Can it tell which change caused the difference? Explain.
5. The Grade 6–8 standard says students plan an investigation about motion, total force, and mass. Which variables and controls should appear in the plan?
6. A cart has a 7 N force to the right and a 7 N force to the left. What is the net force? Are the forces balanced?
7. A cart has 12 N to the right and 5 N to the left. Find the net force and direction.
8. A book is at rest and the vertical forces on it balance. What does the simple model predict next if the net force remains zero?
9. A puck is already sliding north at steady speed. Its net force is zero in the simple model. Is it at rest? What happens to its motion?
10. A cart is moving west while its net force points east. What happens to its westward motion first?
11. For the same cart, what is expected when the net force becomes larger in the same direction?
12. Two carts receive the same net force, but one has greater mass. Which cart is expected to have the smaller change in motion?
13. A student records these observations: Run A moved 42 cm, Run B moved 47 cm, and Run C moved 44 cm. What is the mean distance, to the nearest tenth of a centimeter? These are practice data for calculating a mean, not measurements from the published activity.
14. A group tests three pull strengths but uses a different cart each time. What is one problem with the comparison?
15. A test is repeated three times and the distances are 31 cm, 32 cm, and 60 cm. What should the student report or do about the 60 cm result?
16. Write a claim-evidence-reasoning answer: “How did the tested factor affect the cart's motion?” Use two details from your own table. If the table has no clear pattern, say so rather than forcing a conclusion.

**Checked answers:** 1) The distance traveled by the vehicle. 2) Any two of: car body, ramp, start place, release method, floor/surface, and distance-measurement method. 3) A prediction is written before seeing the new result, so the evidence can fairly support or challenge it. 4) No; two factors changed, so the cause cannot be separated. Repeat with one changed factor. 5) Choose either total force or mass as the factor to change; measure a motion change, hold the other relevant conditions steady, and name the tools, units, and repeats. 6) `0 N`; balanced. 7) `7 N` to the right. 8) It stays at rest in this model. 9) No; it is moving north, and it keeps moving north at the same speed in the zero-net-force model. 10) It slows first because the net force points opposite its westward motion. 11) A larger change in motion, assuming the same object and comparable conditions. 12) The greater-mass cart. 13) `(42+47+44)÷3 = 44.3 cm`. 14) Cart mass, wheel friction, alignment, or construction may differ, so the changed pull is not the only difference. 15) Keep all three results visible; check for a recording or setup error and repeat the trial if possible. Do not discard 60 cm only because it differs. 16) Answers depend on the student's evidence; check that the claim matches the table, cites two real measurements, and gives a reason linked to force and motion. If there is no pattern, an accurate “the data are mixed” claim earns credit.

#### End-of-week check

The student should be able to: (1) find a one-direction net force; (2) explain that balanced forces can go with rest or steady straight motion; (3) explain that unbalanced forces change motion; (4) describe how mass and force affect the amount of change; and (5) plan a fair test with one changed factor, a measured result, controls, and repeated trials. Give one point for each accurate idea and one point for using the student's own evidence with units. For any missed idea, revisit the matching reading or redo the force arrows before repeating the lab explanation.

#### Visuals

![Model diagram comparing balanced opposite forces with an unbalanced rightward force](images/grade-06/science/g06-science-forces-and-motion.png)

Caption: This is a model, not a photograph or a record of a Ditmas experiment. A zero net force means no change in motion in the simple model; it does not mean that every object must be standing still. The linked TeachEngineering page contains a real photo sequence of one Mint-Mobile with four wheels and six wheels. Read its caption and keep the source credit with the image if it is reused on the website.

**Attribution and limits:** The force-and-motion learning target comes from NYSED's published middle-school science standards and the listed MS-PS2-2 performance expectation. The investigation structure and Mint-Mobile details are summarized from the linked TeachEngineering activity and worksheet. This guide adds the labeled tabletop option, force-arrow examples, and practice data; it does not report them as published school materials. Ditmas's actual Grade 6 topic and pacing remain unconfirmed.

Science.title: Science week: Jamaica Bay food links and a changing habitat
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
**Grade-level scope:** New York writes middle-school science expectations for Grades 6–8 as a band, not a separate course calendar for each grade. This week supports MS-LS2-2, modeling patterns of interactions among organisms, and MS-LS2-3, modeling matter and energy flow among living and nonliving parts of an ecosystem. It also studies a human-caused habitat pressure described by the National Park Service, but the NPS pages below do not provide a year-by-year population dataset; students must not claim that this reading alone measures a population decline or proves the size of an effect. Nothing here confirms Ditmas's current unit order or assigned text. [NYSED Middle School Science Learning Standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/standards-instruction/ms-science-learning-standards.pdf).

**Local source case study:** Jamaica Bay is a New York City estuary with beaches, salt marshes, mudflats, and urban neighborhoods nearby. The National Park Service describes how tides and shoreline habitat support living things there. Its species pages document what Atlantic horseshoe crabs eat, where they lay eggs, and how migrating shorebirds use those eggs. These are real relationships for this place, not a claim that every estuary has the same food web. [NPS: Natural Features and Ecosystems at Gateway](https://www.nps.gov/gate/learn/nature/naturalfeaturesandecosystems.htm); [NPS: Atlantic Horseshoe Crab](https://www.nps.gov/articles/ncbn-species-spotlight-atlantic-horseshoe-crab.htm); [NPS: Horseshoe Crabs at Jamaica Bay](https://www.nps.gov/places/000/horseshoe-crabs.htm).

![Jamaica Bay at high tide](https://www.nps.gov/gate/learn/nature/images/IMG_3981_WS.jpg?maxwidth=650&autorotate=false)

*National Park Service photograph of Jamaica Bay at high tide. The picture shows a moment and a place; it does not show all tide stages or all organisms in the bay. [NPS ecosystem page and image credit](https://www.nps.gov/gate/learn/nature/naturalfeaturesandecosystems.htm).*

#### Source reading: follow food and habitat links

An **ecosystem** includes living things and the nonliving parts of a place, such as water, air, light, soil, and temperature. The living things interact with one another and with those nonliving parts. Jamaica Bay has salt marshes, mudflats, beaches, and deeper water. NPS explains that tides move water in and out of the marsh. Incoming tides carry oxygen and nutrients; outgoing tides can leave a line of seaweed and other plant material on shore. This line is called a **wrack line**. NPS says it can shelter crabs and other small animals, which may later become food for gulls. At low tide, exposed mudflats let shorebirds feed on invertebrates. These details show that water level and habitat can affect where organisms find food and shelter. [NPS ecosystem account](https://www.nps.gov/gate/learn/nature/naturalfeaturesandecosystems.htm).

The Atlantic horseshoe crab is part of this local food web. NPS reports that it eats small mollusks, worms, and seaweed from the bottom. Its legs have small spines that help crush food; other small parts move food toward its mouth. In May through July, horseshoe crabs come to sandy beaches around Jamaica Bay to breed and lay eggs. NPS describes the eggs as a food source for migrating shorebirds. The Red Knot is one example: NPS says it travels about 9,000 miles each way between South America and the Canadian Arctic, and it feeds on horseshoe crab eggs during migration. Juvenile fish also depend on the eggs, according to the NPS species account. [NPS Atlantic Horseshoe Crab](https://www.nps.gov/articles/ncbn-species-spotlight-atlantic-horseshoe-crab.htm); [NPS Horseshoe Crabs at Jamaica Bay](https://www.nps.gov/places/000/horseshoe-crabs.htm).

Use an arrow from **food to the organism that eats it**. The documented links in this reading can be drawn like this:

```text
small mollusks, worms, seaweed ──food for──> Atlantic horseshoe crab
horseshoe crab eggs ──food for──> migrating shorebirds, including the Red Knot
wrack line ──shelter for──> crabs and other small animals ──may become food for──> gulls
```

The arrows describe the relationships reported by NPS. In the first two lines, food carries matter and energy into the consumer. The third line shows both shelter and a possible feeding relationship; the wrack line is not itself a predator or a single organism. Some energy is used by organisms and some moves to the surroundings, so the arrows do not mean that all energy passes on unchanged. Do not draw an arrow from one organism to another unless a source supports the relationship.

Habitat matters too. NPS says the number of horseshoe crabs depends in part on having suitable places to spawn. It identifies overharvesting and the loss or hardening of sandy shoreline as pressures; it says losing sandy spawning habitat would make breeding difficult. The linked page says shorebirds and young fish use the eggs as food. Students can use this information to explain a **possible pathway**: less suitable spawning area could make it harder for horseshoe crabs to breed successfully, which could mean fewer eggs are available as food. The source supports those connections but does not give a numeric prediction for the future or prove exactly how many birds or fish would be affected.

#### Evidence table — NPS-reported facts

| Source statement | What a student may conclude | What the statement does not show by itself |
|---|---|---|
| Horseshoe crabs eat small mollusks, worms, and seaweed. | These are documented foods for Atlantic horseshoe crabs in the NPS account. | It does not show that every crab eats the same amount or that these are its only foods. |
| NPS reports that about 3,000 horseshoe crabs come to lay eggs at Plumb Beach. | The account describes a large local spawning event. | It is not a count from every year or a population trend across all of Jamaica Bay. |
| A female may lay about 20,000–30,000 eggs at a time, according to NPS. | The source gives a range rather than one exact number. | It does not mean every egg hatches or survives. |
| Migrating shorebirds, including the Red Knot, feed on the eggs. | There is a documented food link between horseshoe crab eggs and shorebirds. | It does not state how much each bird eats or how many birds depend on one beach. |
| NPS identifies overharvesting and loss/hardening of sandy spawning areas as pressures. | Human actions can affect the physical habitat and horseshoe crab breeding conditions. | These pages alone do not measure the exact change in population caused by each pressure. |

The numbers are quoted as approximate statements from an NPS educational account; they are not measurements collected by the students and are not guaranteed counts for this year. [NPS Atlantic Horseshoe Crab](https://www.nps.gov/articles/ncbn-species-spotlight-atlantic-horseshoe-crab.htm).

#### Five study sessions — about 55–65 minutes each

| Session | Read, model, and practice | Evidence to keep |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Read the ecosystem | Read the source passage and open the NPS ecosystem page. Mark each sentence as a fact about a living thing, a nonliving part, or an interaction. Find the tide, wrack line, mudflat, and horseshoe crab details. Write down two questions the source does not answer. | A two-column list: living/nonliving parts, followed by source facts and questions. |
| 2 — Build a sourced food web | Copy the three verified arrow lines above. Color-code food links and shelter links. Beside every arrow, write the source page that supports it. Add no extra species or arrows unless a reliable source confirms them. Explain why arrows from food to consumer represent matter and energy transfer. | A food-web model with arrows, an evidence label for each connection, and a note about energy leaving the food web to the surroundings. |
| 3 — Check number claims | Study the evidence table. Make a small number line from 20,000 to 30,000 to show the NPS egg range. Calculate the difference between its endpoints. Double-read the words “about,” “at Plumb Beach,” and “at a time”; underline how each phrase limits the claim. | Number line, correct endpoint calculation, and three claim-limit notes. |
| 4 — Trace a habitat change | Use the NPS source to make a cause-and-effect chain from hardening or loss of sandy spawning area to the possible effect on egg-eating shorebirds. Label source statements separately from the student's inference. Add one more link the source supports: juvenile fish also use horseshoe crab eggs. | A chain with facts and inferences visibly distinguished; no invented population count. |
| 5 — Argue from the evidence | Write a claim about why sandy spawning habitat matters in Jamaica Bay. Support it with two NPS details. Explain a limit of the evidence and name one additional kind of data that would help test whether populations changed over time. Finish the question set and teach the food web to someone else. | A claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph, completed questions, and one clearly stated evidence gap. |

#### Supplemental practice — NPS sources and the evidence table

Questions 1–12 check information in the linked NPS accounts. Questions 13–20 use the sourced relationships and guide-created models. They are not Ditmas assignments or copied state-test questions. Any answer about the student's food-web drawing must match the cited arrows above.

1. Name two nonliving parts of Jamaica Bay's ecosystem described in the reading.
2. What is a wrack line?
3. According to NPS, what does an incoming tide bring into the salt marsh?
4. What can the wrack line do for crabs and other small animals?
5. Name the three foods the NPS species account says Atlantic horseshoe crabs eat.
6. How do horseshoe crabs use their legs while feeding, according to NPS?
7. In which months does the NPS account say horseshoe crabs come to Jamaica Bay beaches to breed and lay eggs?
8. Name two kinds of animals that use horseshoe crab eggs as food, according to the NPS source.
9. The NPS account says a female may lay 20,000–30,000 eggs at a time. What is the difference between the two ends of this range?
10. A Red Knot travels about 9,000 miles each way. What is the two-way distance for a trip out and back, if it travels both legs? Show the multiplication.
11. Is “about 3,000 horseshoe crabs come to Plumb Beach” enough to prove their population is growing or shrinking? Why?
12. Name the two pressures on horseshoe crabs identified by NPS in the source reading.
13. In the food web, what do arrows from small mollusks, worms, and seaweed toward a horseshoe crab mean?
14. Why does the food-to-consumer arrow represent both matter and energy transfer?
15. Does the wrack line arrow show a food relationship, a shelter relationship, or both? Explain using the key.
16. Complete the possible cause-and-effect chain: loss/hardening of sandy spawning area → ____ → less egg food may be available to ____.
17. Which part of the habitat-change chain is directly stated by NPS, and which part is a reasonable inference based on two source facts?
18. Name one kind of data that could help test whether horseshoe crab numbers have changed over time.
19. A student adds “small fish are eaten by Red Knots” to the food web. Is that link supported by the sources in this week? What should the student do before adding it?
20. Write a claim about the value of sandy spawning habitat, two source details that support it, and one limit of the source evidence.

#### Checked answer key and evidence guide

1. Examples: **tide/water level, water, sand, beach, mudflat, salt marsh, air, or sunlight.** Name a nonliving part, not an animal or plant.
2. A **wrack line** is a line of seaweed and other plant material left along shore as the tide goes out.
3. NPS says incoming tides bring **oxygen and nutrients** into the marsh.
4. It can provide **shelter** for crabs and other small animals/invertebrates.
5. **Small mollusks, worms, and seaweed.**
6. Small spines on the legs help **crush food**; other small appendages help move it toward the mouth.
7. **May through July.**
8. **Migrating shorebirds** and **juvenile fish**.
9. `30,000 − 20,000 = 10,000`; the range spans **10,000 eggs**.
10. `9,000 × 2 = 18,000`; about **18,000 miles** for the two legs described. This is a calculation from the source's approximate one-way distance, not a measured student's trip.
11. **No.** It is one approximate report for Plumb Beach. To show a trend, a student needs comparable counts from multiple dates or years and must know how they were collected.
12. **Overharvesting** and **loss or hardening of sandy spawning habitat/shoreline**.
13. Those items are **foods eaten by the horseshoe crab**; the arrows point from the food to the consumer.
14. Food contains matter that can become part of an organism; it also transfers stored chemical energy that organisms use. Energy is not passed along unchanged, and some transfers to the surroundings.
15. **Both are shown as separate links.** The wrack line can shelter small animals; the animals may later become food for gulls. The wrack line itself is not the gull's prey in the cited statement.
16. Possible completion: **spawning becomes more difficult for horseshoe crabs** → **migrating shorebirds and juvenile fish**. Say “may” or “could”; the source does not quantify the later effect.
17. NPS directly says loss of sandy spawning habitat would make breeding difficult and that shorebirds/juvenile fish use the eggs as food. The step “fewer successful spawns could mean fewer eggs available as food” is a **reasonable inference**, not a measured population result in this source.
18. **Comparable horseshoe crab counts collected across multiple years** using a consistent method and place; ideally also note survey dates, conditions, and effort.
19. **Not from the sources used here.** Find a reliable species-specific source that documents the feeding link, then cite it before adding the arrow.
20. **Answers vary.** A strong answer names Jamaica Bay's sandy spawning areas, uses two facts such as May–July spawning and eggs as food for shorebirds/juvenile fish, and limits its claim by noting that the source does not measure a current population trend or exact effect size.

**Mastery check:** the learner distinguishes living from nonliving parts, draws only sourced food/habitat links, reads a numerical range accurately, distinguishes a source fact from an inference, explains the possible impact of habitat change without inventing population data, and names what further evidence is needed.

Math.title: Use equivalent ratios
Math.subject: Math
Math.instructions: Study the ratio table and worked examples before solving. Keep the order of the two quantities the same.
Math.explanation: A ratio compares two quantities in a stated order. Equivalent ratios describe the same relationship. To make an equivalent ratio, multiply or divide both quantities by the same nonzero number. If blue beads to yellow beads is 2 to 5, multiplying both parts by 1.5 gives 3 to 7.5. Multiplying both by 2 gives 4 to 10. The relationship stays the same because both parts change by the same factor.

workedExamples.title: Find a value equivalent to 2:5 when the first amount is 3
steps: The first amount changes from 2 to 3, so multiply by 1.5.
Multiply the second amount by the same factor: 5 × 1.5 = 7.5.

workedExamples.title: Scale 4:7 by a factor of 3
steps: Multiply the second part by the same factor: 7 × 3 = 21.
